analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax breaks for the biggest oil companies and doubles tax credits for biofuels and alternative-fuel vehicles.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise taxes on the largest integrated oil companies — those producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude a day — by taking away three tax breaks: favorable write-offs for exploration and drilling costs and the percentage depletion allowance. It would also stop the Interior Department from giving oil and gas producers on federal land a break on their royalty payments whenever oil was above $55 a barrel (with an exception for hurricane disruptions). The money-side flip: it doubles existing tax credits for ethanol, biodiesel, other alternative fuels, hybrid and fuel-cell vehicles, and stations that dispense alternative fuels.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of hybrids, fuel-cell, and other alternative-fuel vehicles would get credits roughly twice as large. Producers and blenders of ethanol, biodiesel, and other alternative fuels would see their per-gallon credits doubled. Owners of fuel stations adding alternative-fuel pumps would get a doubled credit. Taxpayers generally gain from the revenue the oil-company tax changes would raise. Smaller oil and gas producers keep all their existing tax breaks, since the repeal only applies to the biggest integrated companies.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the income and excise tax credits for alcohol (ethanol) fuel, biodiesel, renewable diesel, and other alternative fuel mixtures [S2][S3].

Roughly doubles the credits for buying alternative motor vehicles, including fuel-cell vehicles (top credit rises from $40,000 to $80,000), advanced lean-burn vehicles, hybrids, and alternative-fuel vehicles, and doubles the credit cap for installing alternative-fuel refueling equipment from $30,000 to $60,000 [S3].

Denies major integrated oil companies (500,000+ barrels/day worldwide) the two-year write-off of geological and geophysical costs, the percentage depletion allowance, and the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, effective for tax years after enactment [S2][S3].

Bars the Interior Secretary from using funds to give federal-lands oil and gas producers royalty relief when crude averages over $55 a barrel, except for hurricane or natural-disaster supply disruptions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest integrated oil companies — by scale, firms like those producing half a million barrels or more a day — lose three long-standing tax preferences and the ability to seek royalty relief at high prices. General taxpayers bear the cost of the doubled fuel and vehicle credits, which the bill does not offset with any dedicated revenue source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large integrated oil companies; taxpayers fund doubled credits

drawbacks.text: The doubled fuel and vehicle credits are large new tax expenditures with no offset in the bill, so they add to the deficit rather than being fully paid for by the oil-company provisions [S3].

Blender and producer credits like the ethanol credit historically flow mainly through fuel and agricultural intermediaries, and much of the doubled subsidy could be captured by producers rather than passed to drivers at the pump [S3].

Removing drilling-cost deductions and depletion allowances for the majors could reduce domestic exploration and development spending by the largest companies, an effect supporters would have had to weigh against the added revenue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is taking tax preferences away from the largest oil companies and steering bigger subsidies toward alternative fuels and vehicles. The oil-company provisions raise revenue and close preferences that mainly benefit the biggest firms; the alternative-fuel side is a costly and blunt subsidy instrument whose benefits flow partly to industry intermediaries, and the bill does not pay for it. The royalty-relief ban has a narrow hurricane exception that protects supply in a disaster. On balance the bill favored ordinary taxpayers over the largest oil companies, but the financing was imperfect.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Collins introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Susan Collins introduced S. 2689 in the Senate on May 1, 2006; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor — the bill had zero cosponsors from either party [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major integrated oil companies are better off because the bill died: they kept their depletion allowance, drilling-cost deductions, exploration write-offs, and the possibility of royalty relief at high prices. The ethanol and biodiesel industries are worse off, since their credits were never doubled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies, which kept their tax breaks

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on May 1, 2006; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote after it was referred to Finance; the bill received no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Major integrated oil companies
against.role: Companies averaging 500,000+ barrels of daily worldwide crude production
against.what_they_did: Would have lost their depletion allowance, intangible drilling cost deduction, and exploration write-offs under the bill; the industry actively defended these preferences against comparable measures during the 2006 high-price period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party despite a Republican sponsor, so no partisan split is recorded.

industries.note: Firms producing 500,000+ barrels a day would lose the percentage depletion allowance, the intangible drilling and development cost deduction, and two-year amortization of exploration costs, and could not get federal-lands royalty relief when oil topped $55 a barrel. These preferences are worth billions to the largest firms and are the direct cost the bill imposed on them.

industries.industry: Ethanol and biodiesel producers and blenders
industries.note: The bill doubles the per-gallon credits for alcohol fuels, biodiesel, and renewable diesel. The subsidy flows through fuel intermediaries, so much of the benefit accrues to the industry while drivers see at most a modest pump-price effect.

Credits for fuel-cell, hybrid, lean-burn, and alternative-fuel vehicles roughly double, up to an $80,000 top credit, making advanced-technology vehicles cheaper for buyers and expanding the automakers' market for them.

industries.industry: Independent and small oil and gas producers
industries.note: The repeal applies only to integrated majors at 500,000+ barrels a day, so smaller producers keep their depletion and drilling-cost deductions and gain a relative competitive advantage over the largest firms.
The credit for installing alternative-fuel dispensing property doubles from $30,000 to $60,000 for businesses, encouraging more pumps for ethanol and other alternative fuels.
